title: Word Senses, WordNet and Disambiguation
oneLiner: Many words have several meanings. Learn how meanings relate, how WordNet stores them as a network, and four ways a computer can pick the right one.

what.html:
"I went to the bank": money or river? Words have senses (meanings), and senses relate to each other (synonyms, opposites, general and specific kinds, parts and wholes). WordNet stores all of this as a big network of meanings. Word sense disambiguation uses the surrounding words to choose which meaning a sentence uses.

Everyday versionA multiple-choice question: the senses are options A, B, C; the words around the ambiguous one are the clues you use to pick.

why.html:
• Search, translation and question answering go wrong if they pick the wrong meaning.
  • Knowing that a bat (the animal) is a mammal gives a computer lots of facts for free.
  • The same "compare with definitions" trick powers modern semantic search.

how.title: Forms, entries, meanings
how.html: "running" and "ran" share the dictionary form "run"; "run" itself has several meanings (move fast, manage a company, an engine running).

how.title: Unrelated or related meanings?
how.html: A cricket bat and a flying bat are unrelated (homonymy). A newspaper and a question paper are both still paper (polysemy).

how.title: How words relate
how.html: big/large (synonyms), rich/poor (opposites), vehicle → car → SUV (general to specific), wheel → car (part of).

how.title: Meaning groups
how.html: WordNet groups synonyms into one meaning node: {intelligent, clever, bright, brilliant, smart}. Verbs and adjectives get their own kinds of links (snoring is a way of sleeping; hot is the opposite of cold).

how.title: A dictionary as a network
how.html: The two "bat" meanings sit in different branches: one under mammal, one under sports equipment. Position tells you meaning, and closeness in the network measures similarity.

how.title: Just guess the usual meaning
how.html: If 80% of uses mean the cricket bat, always guessing it is right 80% of the time, but never in "the bat flew out of the cave".

how.title: Learn from labelled examples
how.html: From hand-labelled sentences, learn which words go with each meaning. "approved" and "loan" make the money meaning about 28 times more likely than the river meaning.

how.title: Compare meanings as vectors
how.html: Turn the sentence and each definition into vectors and pick the closest: "The bank approved my loan" is near "financial institution that lends money".

how.title: Count shared words with definitions
how.html: The Lesk method counts words the sentence shares with each dictionary definition, like a recruiter matching keywords in a CV. Simple, but "fisherman" doesn't literally match "fish".

demo.html: Match each description to the disambiguation method it describes.

example.html:
Naive Bayes, by hand. Money sense: 0.8 (prior) × 5/16 (loan) × 3/16 (approved) = 0.0469. River sense: 0.2 × 1/11 × 1/11 = 0.0017. The money meaning wins by about 28 times; adding 1 to every count stopped the river meaning from scoring exactly zero.

Supplementary Within one document a word usually keeps the same meaning ("one sense per discourse"), a handy shortcut for disambiguating long texts.

misunderstandings: It only finds the base form.
Same spelling means same WordNet node.
Each sense is a separate synset.
Plain Lesk needs exact word overlap.
takeaways: Lexeme (entry), lemma (base form), sense (meaning), synset (synonym group).
Synonym, antonym, hypernym/hyponym, meronym; relations vary by part of speech.
WordNet = dictionary as a graph: inheritance and path similarity.
WSD: most frequent sense, Naive Bayes (28×), embeddings, Lesk.
thirty: Word + context = meaning (bank: money vs river). Lexeme = entry; lemma = citation form (run for ran/running); sense = one meaning; synset = synonym set {intelligent, clever, bright, brilliant, smart}. Homonymy: unrelated meanings (bat, match); polysemy: related (paper, mouth). Relations: synonyms (big/large, not perfectly substitutable), antonyms (hot/cold), hypernym/hyponym (vehicle → car → SUV), meronym (wheel/car); verbs have troponymy (snore/sleep) and entailment. WordNet = lexical database as a graph; bat₁ under mammal, bat₂ under sports equipment; inheritance; path similarity (bat₁–dog 1/3, bat₁–bat₂ 1/7). WSD: most-frequent-sense baseline (80%); Naive Bayes with add-1 (finance 0.8 × 0.3125 × 0.1875 = 0.0469 vs river 0.0017, ≈ 28×); embedding similarity (cos 0.98 vs 0.49); Lesk gloss overlap (loan ~ loans → finance; fisherman/bass shows brittleness; extended Lesk, stemming, embeddings fix it).

Lesk picks the sense whose gloss…
opts: Shares the most words with the context
